name: Khirwar

earlier_scan.note: Sole reference is Crooke 1896 ethnographic chapter; no linguistic description of Khirwar exists

new_statements.quote: आदिवासी अन्य स्थानीय वक्ताओं की तरह ही स्वरों का उच्चारण करते हैं, लेकिन भोजपुरी क्षेत्र क्रिया रूपों को जब स्वरान्त बनाता है तो शब्द के अन्त में प्रयुक्त /अ/ स्वर केवल क्रिया रूप में संवृत रूप में उच्चरित होता है, तथा यह अर्थभेदक होने लगता है। जैसे - चल् और चल॑ ; जर् और जर॑ । इस स्थिति में /चल॑/ और /जर॑/ आज्ञार्थक क्रियायें हैं, जिसका अर्थ है - चलो तथा जलो। /जर्/ में बलाघात /ज/ पर है। इस कारण शब्द का अर्थ है - बुखार। /जर॑/ में बलाघात /र/ पर है, जिसका अर्थ है - जलो। इस तरह यह बलाघात भी अर्थभेदक दिखाई पड़ता है। दीर्घता आदिवासियों में नहीं मिलती।
new_statements.translation: The Adivasis pronounce the vowels just as other local speakers do, but where the Bhojpuri area makes verb forms vowel-final, the /a/ used at the end of the word is pronounced as a close vowel only in the verb form, and this becomes distinctive. E.g. cal vs cal-a, jar vs jar-a. Here /cal-a/ and /jar-a/ are imperative verbs meaning 'go!' and 'burn!'. In /jar/ the stress is on /ja/, hence the word means 'fever'. In /jar-a/ the stress is on /ra/, and it means 'burn!'. Thus this stress too appears to be meaning-distinguishing. (Vowel) length is not found among the Adivasis. [Earlier, p. 43: 'Baswar, Khairwar and Kol also speak the local language today, but their pronunciation, accent (स्वराघात) and manner of expression are somewhat different.']

Passage found at the scanned text (sec. 3.3 'खण्डेतर ध्वनिग्राम', thesis pp. 65-66) exactly where A says; A's quote matches the scanned word for word apart from scanned noise; the sentence naming 'गोड, खरवार व बसवार जातियां' immediately precedes it, and the p. 43 remark on Baswar/Khairwar/Kol 'उच्चारण, स्वराघात.. थोडा अलग' is at the scanned text. new_statements.relation_note: see quote; no tone; length non-distinctive; nasalization phonemic
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Bhojpuri-Bagheli speech of Sonbhadra Gond/Kharwar/Baswar the only suprasegmental statements are: nasalization is phonemic; stress (बलाघात) is said to be distinctive at least in noun vs imperative pairs - jar 'fever' stressed on the first syllable vs jar-a 'burn!' stressed on the final syllable (whose final -a is pronounced close); vowel length is not distinctive. No default stress position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the contrast is illustrated only with cal/cal-a and jar/jar-a (noun or bare stem vs imperative)
new_statements.identity_note: Describes the speech of the Adivasi communities of Sonbhadra district (UP; = Crooke 1896's 'South Mirzapur', the locus of Glottolog's only khir1237 reference), immediately north of Surguja: Dhangar (Kurux-related, own language) versus Gond, Kharwar/Khairwar (खरवार/खैरवार), Baswar, Agaria, Panika etc., who are stated to speak a Bhojpuri-Bagheli mixed Indo-Aryan variety with their own pronunciation and accent. So it is first-hand data on the speech of the Kharwar population that the code kwx names, but that speech is Indo-Aryan (Bhojpuri bhoj1244 / Bagheli bagh1251 type), not a Dravidian language; whether this counts as 'Khirwar' depends on whether khir1237 is taken as the (probably spurious) Dravidian entity or as the actual speech of the Kharwar/Khirwar people.

readall_conflicts: No source opened in this or the earlier reading makes any statement about word stress in Khirwar, so there is no stress disagreement. There is an identity conflict between the database entry and the census: Ethnologue/Glottolog place a Dravidian 'Khirwar' (alt. Kalari, Kherwari, Khirwara) in Surguja, but Census 2011 shows 'Kalari' (Gondi group) concentrated in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra with zero returns in Surguja, and the Surguja Khairwar tribe returning Indo-Aryan mother tongues (Surgujia, Sadri, Bhojpuri, Hindi) almost exclusively; LSI Jharkhand 2023 likewise marks the Kharwar as having 'completely given up their own mother tongue' in favour of Nagpuria, and Russell & Hira Lal 1916 (earlier reading) said the same for the Central Provinces Khairwar. Grierson's 'Kherwari' is a Munda label (Santali-Mundari-Ho), unrelated.
